name: Aaron Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does an ordinary day at your accounting firm look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Aaron, 27, and I lead the tax review desk. I have a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I spend the morning tracing entries back to bank statements before signing returns. I like finding an error early, but I dislike clients being promised a deadline before anyone sees the books.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do money and new tools fit into your life now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My pay is higher than most accountants at my level and I have about nine months of expenses saved. My partner Noor and I rent while saving for a house, and plenty of accounting firms operate nearby. I have never used AI tools; I want a process I can explain to a client rather than a quick answer I cannot trace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A modest receipt tool would not change my week very much. The tax calendar would still set the rhythm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team to let the software sort duplicates if someone can show its workings. I would still sign a return only after my own review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is secure in this picture, and I have nine months of expenses saved. My pay is above the usual rate, with plenty of firms nearby, so I can afford to say no to a poor process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same client review rota and use my existing checklist through the next tax season. I would also put a fixed part of each monthly salary into the house deposit account I already hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and money here. The most irritating risk is a rushed return, not losing the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you skip a tool that saves time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool and do not know enough to trust one with a client ledger. I am willing to look at a proper error report when the firm has one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the deposit a new plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have been saving for a small place for a year. I would keep transferring the same amount rather than enlarge the plan because software saved a few minutes.

say: I would let software sort **duplicates** if its workings are visible.
I would keep my own **final review** before signing tax returns.
think: Nine months of savings and **higher pay** leave my job and rent secure.
I can reject a weak **review process** because many local firms hire accountants.
do: Keep my **client review rota** and checklist through tax season.
Transfer a fixed **salary amount** into my existing house deposit each month.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, pay, and the flat.
S0.quote: I would still sign a return only after my own review.
fieldNote: He has **never used AI**, but leaves room to inspect evidence of a tool’s errors.
Strong savings, high pay, and **many nearby firms** make his caution practical rather than desperate.

steps.text: Keep the client review rota and personal checklist
Transfer a fixed salary amount into house deposit monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Draft returns and checks are the spine of our office. I would want more than a sales pitch before we change the sign-off process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we should compare the software against old returns with known mistakes and keep the person who signs accountable. If staff hours change, the firm should put the new figures on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry that fewer juniors will mean a narrower path into senior accounting, and my own review hours could shrink if clients pay less. My savings let me wait for the evidence, but I do not want my signature to become the only thing left of my accounting job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask my manager Elin to fund a controlled test on fifty old returns; I would read the error report, not run the AI myself yet. If our own hours are cut in the first year of the change, I would apply to a posted senior accountant vacancy with a stated salary at least as high as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the work becoming thinner, though my bank account gives me time. I would rather make one sound move than chase a new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check those fifty returns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pair an experienced reviewer with a trainee and compare both records with the software output. The test belongs on paid work time, because clients should not fund an unpaid experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the test looks strong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a supervised class if the firm paid for it and the audit trail remained visible. I am slow with new tools, but a good record could change my mind.

say: I would demand a **fifty-return test** with known mistakes and human sign-off.
I would ask management to publish **staffing figures** if hours change.
think: My own **review hours** could shrink as clients pay less.
Savings let me inspect the **evidence** before changing firms.
do: Request a **paid controlled test** on fifty old returns.
Take a **supervised AI class** only if the test succeeds and the firm pays.
Apply for an **equal-or-higher-paid** senior vacancy if my hours are cut.
feel: I feel **anxious** about shrinking hours, with financial room to respond.
S1.quote: I do not want my signature to become the only thing left of my accounting job.
fieldNote: He will consider learning AI only after a **controlled paid test** with known errors.
His job search is **conditional** on reduced hours and a posted vacancy that preserves salary.

steps.text: Wait for paid fifty-return test report before deciding whether to use AI
Take firm-paid supervised AI class only after successful test
Apply for posted senior vacancies paying at least current salary if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is shorter than a full trainee cycle in our firm. There is no comfort in the robots being later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that AGI reaching our accounts and tax returns in 2028 calls for a real client liability plan. Robots around 2031 will not delay a desk-based cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect most preparation fees to vanish and my senior review post to be cut. Nine months of savings and nearby firms help, but I cannot assume another firm will keep the same pay when every tax desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would pause the house search and redirect my monthly deposit transfer into a liquid emergency account. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for advertised tax dispute roles with a published salary; I would accept a lower salary only after calculating how long the reserve could cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect to lose the job I trained for. I can carry rent for a while, but that does not make the cut imaginary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Noor that I am delaying the house purchase, not abandoning it. We would keep the present lease until my income is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start an AI course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from a glossy advert. I would ask Elin for paid time to observe a tested system, but I would not enrol without a course that shows its errors and client safeguards.

say: I would demand a **client liability plan** for the 2028 desk change.
I would say robots arriving around **2031** cannot postpone accounting cuts.
think: I expect my **senior review post** and much preparation fee work to vanish.
Nine months saved buys time, but local firms may cut **similar desks**.
do: Redirect my **house deposit transfer** into a liquid emergency account.
Delay the **house purchase** and renew our current lease.
Seek **advertised tax dispute posts** after job loss; accept lower pay only after calculating how long reserves cover rent.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected job loss despite a reserve.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings and nearby firms help, but I cannot assume another firm will keep the same pay when every tax desk changes.
fieldNote: He distinguishes the **2028 screen-work shock** from robots arriving around 2031.
He redirects new monthly saving to cash; a lower-paid vacancy is acceptable only after **calculating rent coverage**.

steps.text: Redirect monthly deposit contribution into liquid emergency savings
Delay house purchase and renew current lease
Apply for advertised salaried tax dispute roles if senior post ends
Accept lower salary only after calculating how long reserves cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give me more than a sales demo to judge. I could watch what happens to actual client fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team that our 2031 desk work remains exposed, even though robots come around 2034. The firm should publish which review duties it expects people to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect the routine fee base to shrink, but five years lets me test another paid line of work while keeping my salary. My resistance to AI is not a belief that clients will pay forever for the same return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Elin for paid access to one tax dispute case each quarter and complete the professional body’s disputes module if she pays the fee. In the first year after 2031 I would move into a salaried dispute post only if a firm actually advertises one; otherwise I would keep my current role while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the change, but five years makes the training decision less rushed. I would not borrow against a job that may not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as useful training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to follow a case from a client notice through the final answer, with an experienced accountant checking me. A module alone would not show whether I can do that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the flat deposit investments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit is cash, not a share bet. I would keep adding to an emergency account from salary and review the balance before any voluntary job move.

say: I would ask for **published review duties** before the 2031 change.
I would separate **2031 desk exposure** from robots arriving around 2034.
think: Routine tax **fees** may shrink even with five years of warning.
I could test paid **dispute work** while keeping my senior salary.
do: Complete a **funded disputes module** and follow paid quarterly casework only if Elin approves fees and access.
Keep adding **monthly salary savings** to the emergency account.
Move after **2031** to an advertised salaried disputes post after reviewing cash; otherwise keep my paid role.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to judge a real alternative.
S3.quote: I would not borrow against a job that may not exist.
fieldNote: His retraining requires a **funded module** and supervised paid casework, not a speculative certificate.
He keeps saving from **current salary** and requires an advertised salaried post before moving.

steps.text: Complete firm-funded disputes module and paid quarterly casework only with Elin approval
Transfer a fixed salary amount into emergency savings monthly
Move to advertised salaried disputes post after 2031 only after reviewing emergency cash balance
Keep current role while it pays if no salaried disputes post is advertised

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade would let me finish a long plan instead of guessing at every announcement. I would still want written proof before changing the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI changes accounts desks by 2036 and robots follow around 2039, so we should plan on the earlier date. Ten years also gives firms time to train people honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my present role could still contract, but at 37 I could have a larger reserve and actual dispute cases behind me. With good pay and many nearby firms, I would not trade that for an invented title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue reviewing returns now and set aside a fixed monthly amount from salary until I have a full year of expenses. I would take paid dispute cases only if Elin assigns them; in the first year after 2036 I would take an advertised salaried dispute role if my review post contracts and the pay covers our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, though a ten-year plan is something I can live with. I would worry more about the younger accountants with no chance to learn judgment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a proven tool became part of firm work, I would take paid supervised training before handling a client return with it. I would not volunteer a live file as the test case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the trainees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Elin to keep a paid training place where juniors check real records under a senior reviewer. Without a paid trainee place, the firm would be borrowing skill from a generation it never trained.

say: I would plan against the **2036 desk date**, not the later 2039 robot date.
I would ask the firm to keep a **paid trainee place** with real records.
think: My current role may **contract**, but ten years allows genuine dispute experience.
A full-year **cash reserve** and nearby firms would give me choices.
do: Save a fixed **salary amount** until one year of expenses is covered.
Take **paid dispute cases** only if Elin assigns them.
Take an **advertised disputes role** after 2036 only if review work contracts and salary covers rent.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the desk job, with time and money to plan.
S4.quote: Without a paid trainee place, the firm would be borrowing skill from a generation it never trained.
fieldNote: His long runway rests on **new monthly saving** and assigned casework, not an assumed future salary.
He considers AI learning only after a **proven system** and paid supervised instruction.

steps.text: Save fixed salary amount until one year of expenses is covered
Take paid supervised AI training if proven tool enters firm work
Take advertised disputes job after 2036 if review work contracts and pay covers rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the firm to cut the review desk before other paid work is ready. An honest liability plan, a funded way to learn dispute cases, and early notice of cuts would help. I would still need a real vacancy and a rent-covering salary before changing roles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who will train the next accountant. A tax return is not just a number on a screen when a client has to explain it to an authority. I want juniors to learn from real mistakes while there is still a reviewer to guide them.

headlineQuote: A tax return is not just a number on a screen when a client has to explain it to an authority.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** team lead with a master’s degree and chartered qualification who checks tax returns.
He has **higher pay**, nine months saved, a partner, and many nearby accounting firms.
He has **never used AI** and wants evidence, audit trails, and paid supervision before using it.
He delays a **house purchase** in a fast shock and redirects new monthly saving to cash.
His **2028** job loss expectation alarms him; longer runways support funded dispute learning and a larger reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his senior review desk before another paid role is ready.
whatWouldHelp: He wants an honest **liability plan**, funded dispute learning, early notice, and a real vacancy with rent-covering pay.
